claim: Malaria-transmitting mosquitoes cause over 245 million malaria cases annually.
source: Malaria-transmitting mosquitoes cause over 245 million malaria cases and about 620,000 deaths annually (WHO, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO, 2021

claim: Malaria-transmitting mosquitoes cause about 620,000 deaths annually.
source: Malaria-transmitting mosquitoes cause over 245 million malaria cases and about 620,000 deaths annually (WHO, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO, 2021

claim: Vector control has permitted a steady decrease in malaria cases during the last decades.
source: Vector control, mainly in the form of insecticide indoor residual spraying and insecticide-treated bed nets, has permitted a steady decrease in malaria cases during the last decades.
evidence: Stated as established fact in the introduction

claim: The decline in malaria cases is stalling as mosquitoes become increasingly resistant to insecticides.
source: However, this decline is stalling as mosquitoes become increasingly resistant to insecticides and as malaria parasites continue to evolve resistance to drugs.
evidence: Stated as established fact in the introduction

claim: Malaria parasites continue to evolve resistance to drugs.
source: However, this decline is stalling as mosquitoes become increasingly resistant to insecticides and as malaria parasites continue to evolve resistance to drugs.
evidence: Stated as established fact in the introduction

claim: Lipophorin is an essential, highly expressed lipid transport protein that is secreted and circulates in insect hemolymph.
source: Lipophorin is an essential, highly expressed lipid transport protein that is secreted and circulates in insect hemolymph.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript

claim: The Anopheles coluzzii Lipophorin gene was hijacked to co-express a single-chain version of antibody 2A10.
source: We hijacked the Anopheles coluzzii Lipophorin gene to make it co-express a single-chain version of antibody 2A10, which binds sporozoites of the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum.
evidence: Described as the main experimental approach in the abstract

claim: Antibody 2A10 binds sporozoites of the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum.
source: We hijacked the Anopheles coluzzii Lipophorin gene to make it co-express a single-chain version of antibody 2A10, which binds sporozoites of the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum.
evidence: Supported by citation to Zavala et al., 1983 in the introduction

claim: Transgenic mosquitoes with Lp::Sc2A10 show a markedly decreased ability to transmit Plasmodium berghei expressing the P. falciparum circumsporozoite protein to mice.
source: The resulting transgenic mosquitoes show a markedly decreased ability to transmit Plasmodium berghei expressing the P. falciparum circumsporozoite protein to mice.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and described in Results section

claim: A CRISPR/Cas9-based gene drive was designed and installed in the Saglin gene.
source: To force the spread of this antimalarial transgene in a mosquito population, we designed and tested several CRISPR/Cas9-based gene drives. One of these is installed in, and disrupts, the pro-parasitic gene Saglin and also cleaves wild-type Lipophorin, causing the anti-malarial modified Lipophorin version to replace the wild type and hitch-hike together with the Saglin drive.
evidence: Described as experimental approach in abstract and detailed in Results

claim: The Saglin-based gene drive disrupts the pro-parasitic gene Saglin.
source: One of these is installed in, and disrupts, the pro-parasitic gene Saglin and also cleaves wild-type Lipophorin, causing the anti-malarial modified Lipophorin version to replace the wild type and hitch-hike together with the Saglin drive.
evidence: Described in abstract and demonstrated in Results section

claim: The Saglin-based gene drive cleaves wild-type Lipophorin.
source: One of these is installed in, and disrupts, the pro-parasitic gene Saglin and also cleaves wild-type Lipophorin, causing the anti-malarial modified Lipophorin version to replace the wild type and hitch-hike together with the Saglin drive.
evidence: Described in abstract and demonstrated in Results section

claim: The Saglin-based gene drive generates drive-resistant alleles.
source: Although generating drive-resistant alleles and showing instability in its gRNA-encoding multiplex array, the Saglin-based gene drive reached high levels in caged mosquito populations and efficiently promoted the simultaneous spread of the antimalarial Lipophorin::Sc2A10 allele.
evidence: Demonstrated by sequencing data in Figure 8 and described in Results

claim: The Saglin-based gene drive shows instability in its gRNA-encoding multiplex array.
source: Although generating drive-resistant alleles and showing instability in its gRNA-encoding multiplex array, the Saglin-based gene drive reached high levels in caged mosquito populations and efficiently promoted the simultaneous spread of the antimalarial Lipophorin::Sc2A10 allele.
evidence: Demonstrated by PCR and sequencing data in Figure 9 and described in Results

claim: The Saglin-based gene drive reached high levels in caged mosquito populations.
source: Although generating drive-resistant alleles and showing instability in its gRNA-encoding multiplex array, the Saglin-based gene drive reached high levels in caged mosquito populations and efficiently promoted the simultaneous spread of the antimalarial Lipophorin::Sc2A10 allele.
evidence: Demonstrated by COPAS data in Figure 7 and described in Results

claim: The Saglin-based gene drive efficiently promoted the simultaneous spread of the antimalarial Lipophorin::Sc2A10 allele.
source: Although generating drive-resistant alleles and showing instability in its gRNA-encoding multiplex array, the Saglin-based gene drive reached high levels in caged mosquito populations and efficiently promoted the simultaneous spread of the antimalarial Lipophorin::Sc2A10 allele.
evidence: Demonstrated by COPAS data in Figure 7 and described in Results

claim: The combination of Saglin disruption and Lp::Sc2A10 is expected to decrease parasite transmission via two different mechanisms.
source: This combination is expected to decrease parasite transmission via two different mechanisms.
evidence: Based on logical inference from the known functions of Saglin and Sc2A10

claim: Lipophorin and Vitellogenin are the two most abundant proteins secreted in Anopheles hemolymph.
source: The two most abundant proteins secreted in Anopheles hemolymph are the nutrient transporters Lipophorin (Lp) and Vitellogenin (Vg), as illustrated by Coomassie staining of electrophoresis gels revealing both proteins as the major visible bands in hemolymph extracts (Figure 1A and Rono et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by Coomassie staining data in Figure 1A and citation to Rono et al., 2010

claim: Vitellogenin is induced in mosquito females only upon blood feeding and wanes within 3 days as eggs develop.
source: While Vg is induced in mosquito females only upon blood feeding and wanes within 3 days as eggs develop, Lp is expressed constitutively, with a further spike of expression after blood feeding (Attardo et al., 2005; Rono et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Attardo et al., 2005 and Rono et al., 2010

claim: Lipophorin is expressed constitutively, with a further spike of expression after blood feeding.
source: While Vg is induced in mosquito females only upon blood feeding and wanes within 3 days as eggs develop, Lp is expressed constitutively, with a further spike of expression after blood feeding (Attardo et al., 2005; Rono et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Attardo et al., 2005 and Rono et al., 2010

claim: Sc2A10 was knocked-in in frame after the endogenous first Lp coding exon using the CRISPR-Cas9 system.
source: Using the CRISPR-Cas9 system, we knocked-in codon-optimized Sc2A10 in frame after the endogenous first Lp coding exon, which encodes the Lp secretion signal peptide (Figure 1B, for sequence of the plasmid used for knock-in see Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: Described in Results section and illustrated in Figure 1B

claim: A natural furin proteolytic cleavage site located between the ApoLpII and ApoLpI subunits of the Lp polypeptide allows their separation during maturation in the Golgi apparatus.
source: A natural furin proteolytic cleavage site located between the ApoLpII and ApoLpI subunits of the Lp polypeptide allows their separation during maturation in the Golgi apparatus (Smolenaars et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Smolenaars et al., 2005

claim: The furin cleavage site was duplicated to detach Sc2A10 from ApoLpII during protein maturation.
source: We duplicated this motif to detach Sc2A10 from ApoLpII during protein maturation.
evidence: Described as part of the experimental design in Results

claim: Silent mutations were introduced in the majority of possible Cas9 sgRNA target sites within Lp exon 1 and the beginning of intron 1.
source: The knock-in design also introduced silent mutations in the majority of possible Cas9 sgRNA target sites within Lp exon 1 and the beginning of intron 1, to facilitate selection of multiple sgRNAs targeting WT Lp, but not its engineered allele, when designing subsequent GDs.
evidence: Described as part of the experimental design in Results

claim: A GFP marker gene under control of the synthetic 3xP3 promoter was placed in the first intron of Lp.
source: Finally, the 1644-bp first intron immediately following Lp exon 1 offered an ideal location to host a fluorescent selection marker to identify and track the modified gene. We placed a GFP marker gene under control of the synthetic 3xP3 promoter (Horn and Wimmer, 2000) and D. melanogaster Tubulin56D terminator in this intron, with care taken to preserve the intron splice junctions and in reverse orientation relative to Lp transcription so that the Tub56D terminator would not cause premature arrest of Lp mRNA transcription.
evidence: Described as part of the experimental design in Results

claim: The homozygous Lp::Sc2A10 stock was fertile and viable, devoid of obvious fitness cost.
source: The homozygous stock was fertile and viable, devoid of obvious fitness cost.
evidence: Based on observation of mosquito populations in the laboratory

claim: The Lp::Sc2A10 transgene shows slow disappearance over time indicative of a subtle fitness cost that decreased transgene frequency by an average of 2.3% each generation.
source: A more careful evaluation of Lp::Sc2A10 fitness costs was conducted by following the dynamics of the transgene in the heterozygous population over 17 generations. This revealed slow disappearance of the transgene over time (Figure 1C and Supplementary file 2) indicative of a subtle fitness cost that decreased transgene frequency by an average of 2.3% each generation.
evidence: Demonstrated by COPAS data in Figure 1C and Supplementary file 2

claim: Homozygous transgenic Lp::Sc2A10 females consistently engendered fewer progeny than their WT sisters.
source: In fertility assays comparing WT and homozygous transgenic females, the latter consistently engendered fewer progeny than their WT sisters, pointing to a negative impact of the Lp modification on their reproductive capacity (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by fertility assay data in Supplementary file 3

claim: Sc2A10 peptides were detected in hemolymph from homozygous transgenic mosquitoes by mass spectrometry.
source: To test whether the Sc2A10 single-chain antibody was expressed and secreted in hemolymph via the Lp signal peptide, we extracted hemolymph from transgenic female mosquitoes and analyzed its protein content by mass spectrometry.
evidence: Demonstrated by mass spectrometry data in Table 1

claim: In hemolymph from homozygous transgenic mosquitoes, for a total of 2629 peptides from ApoLpI, 672 peptides from ApoLpII and 18 from Sc2A10 were detected.
source: In two mass spectrometry samples from the hemolymph of homozygous transgenic mosquitoes, for a total of 2629 peptides from the largest Lp subunit ApoLpI, we detected 672 peptides from smaller ApoLpII and 18 from Sc2A10 (Table 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by mass spectrometry data in Table 1

claim: Sc2A10 molecules are 10- to 20-fold less abundant in the hemolymph compared to ApoLpI and ApoLpII.
source: Corrected for size, this suggests that Sc2A10 molecules are 10- to 20-fold less abundant in the hemolymph compared to ApoLpI and ApoLpII.
evidence: Inferred from mass spectrometry data in Table 1

claim: Western blots using anti-ApoLpII antibodies on hemolymph samples from homozygous transgenic mosquitoes showed no size upshift for ApoLpII, confirming that Sc2A10 is properly released from ApoLpII.
source: Of note, western blots using anti-ApoLpII antibodies on hemolymph samples from homozygous transgenic mosquitoes showed no size upshift for ApoLpII, confirming that Sc2A10 is properly released from ApoLpII (Figure 1D).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot data in Figure 1D

claim: Higher Lp concentrations were observed in heterozygous compared to homozygous mosquitoes.
source: Overall, we observed higher Lp concentrations in heterozygous compared to homozygous mosquitoes, and a three to fourfold lower Sc2A10: Lp ratio in heterozygotes compared to homozygotes, indicating that the chimeric proteins from Lp::Sc2A10 are less expressed than from WT Lp.
evidence: Inferred from mass spectrometry data in Table 1

claim: The chimeric proteins from Lp::Sc2A10 are less expressed than from WT Lp.
source: Overall, we observed higher Lp concentrations in heterozygous compared to homozygous mosquitoes, and a three to fourfold lower Sc2A10: Lp ratio in heterozygotes compared to homozygotes, indicating that the chimeric proteins from Lp::Sc2A10 are less expressed than from WT Lp.
evidence: Inferred from mass spectrometry data in Table 1

claim: Only 29.7% (11/37) of mice exposed to Lp::Sc2A10 homozygous infected mosquitoes developed parasitemia, compared to 97.1% (33/34) exposed to infected control mosquitoes.
source: Only 29.7% (11/37) of mice exposed to Lp::Sc2A10 homozygous infected mosquitoes developed parasitemia, compared to 97.1% (33/34) exposed to infected control mosquitoes (Figure 2A and Supplementary file 4A).
evidence: Demonstrated by bite-back experiment data in Figure 2A and Supplementary file 4A

claim: Sc2A10 significantly reduced transmission of Pb-PfCSP (p<0.0001).
source: Consistent with previous reports (Isaacs et al., 2011; Isaacs et al., 2012; Sumitani et al., 2013), Sc2A10 significantly reduced transmission of Pb-PfCSP (p<0.0001).
evidence: Demonstrated by bite-back experiment data in Figure 2A and statistical analysis

claim: Six of the 11 mice that did become infected by transgenic mosquitoes experienced a 1 day delay in the development of detectable parasitemia in the blood.
source: Additionally, 6 of the 11 mice that did become infected by transgenic mosquitoes experienced a 1 day delay in the development of detectable parasitemia in the blood (Supplementary file 4A), indicative of reduced liver infection (Reuling et al., 2020).
evidence: Demonstrated by bite-back experiment data in Supplementary file 4A and supported by citation to Reuling et al., 2020

claim: Only 4 out of 12 mice bitten by heterozygous mosquitoes became infected, compared to 17 out of 18 mice bitten by control mosquitoes.
source: While 17 out of 18 mice bitten by control mosquitoes became infected, only 4 out of 12 mice bitten by heterozygous mosquitoes became infected (Figure 2B and Supplementary file 4B).
evidence: Demonstrated by bite-back experiment data in Figure 2B and Supplementary file 4B

claim: Heterozygous mosquitoes showed a statistically significant reduction in transmission compared to wild-type (p=0.0006).
source: Two-tailed Fisher's exact test shows a statistically significant reduction when comparing wild-type and heterozygous (p=0.0006) mosquitoes regarding their Plasmodium-transmitting capacity.
evidence: Demonstrated by statistical analysis of bite-back experiment data

claim: Heterozygous mosquitoes showed a transmission blocking activity comparable to that seen in homozygotes.
source: Therefore, heterozygous mosquitoes showed a transmission blocking activity comparable to that seen in homozygotes.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of bite-back experiment data in Figures 2A and 2B

claim: Lp::Sc2A10 and wild-type mosquitoes transmitted the control P. berghei strain to mice with equal efficiencies (n=5/5 and 4/4 mice infected, respectively).
source: While Lp::Sc2A10 and wild-type mosquitoes transmitted the control P. berghei strain to mice with equal efficiencies (n=5/5 and 4/4 mice infected, respectively), only the WT mosquitoes transmitted Pb-PfCSPhsp70-GFP (n=3/3 mice infected), whereas Lp::Sc2A10 mosquitoes blocked transmission of the PfCSP-expressing strain (n=0/4 mice infected).
evidence: Demonstrated by bite-back experiment data in Figure 2C and Supplementary file 4C

claim: Only the WT mosquitoes transmitted Pb-PfCSPhsp70-GFP (n=3/3 mice infected), whereas Lp::Sc2A10 mosquitoes blocked transmission of the PfCSP-expressing strain (n=0/4 mice infected).
source: While Lp::Sc2A10 and wild-type mosquitoes transmitted the control P. berghei strain to mice with equal efficiencies (n=5/5 and 4/4 mice infected, respectively), only the WT mosquitoes transmitted Pb-PfCSPhsp70-GFP (n=3/3 mice infected), whereas Lp::Sc2A10 mosquitoes blocked transmission of the PfCSP-expressing strain (n=0/4 mice infected).
evidence: Demonstrated by bite-back experiment data in Figure 2C and Supplementary file 4C

claim: The transmission blocking capacity of the Sc2A10 transgene is PfCSP-specific.
source: This indicates that the transmission blocking capacity of the Sc2A10 transgene is indeed PfCSP-specific (Figure 2C and Supplementary file 4C).
evidence: Inferred from bite-back experiment data in Figure 2C and Supplementary file 4C

claim: Saglin knockout mutants bear no fitness cost at least in laboratory conditions.
source: Because Saglin knockout mutants bear no fitness cost at least in laboratory conditions, GD-refractory Saglin alleles generated by failed homing events are certain to accumulate over time
evidence: Supported by citation to Klug et al., 2023

claim: A Lp suppression GD was constructed with an array of 4 gRNAs targeting Lp but not Lp::Sc2A10, expressed under control of a single U6 promoter.
source: We constructed a DsRedNLS-marked Lp suppression GD (Figure 3A and annotated sequence in Supplementary file 1C), in which an array of 4 gRNAs separated by tRNAs (Xie et al., 2015; Port and Bullock, 2016), targeting Lp but not Lp::Sc2A10, were expressed under control of a single U6 promoter.
evidence: Described as experimental design in Results and illustrated in Figure 3A

claim: Cas9 was placed under the control of zpg regulatory elements in the Lp suppression GD.
source: Cas9 was placed under the control of zpg regulatory elements, currently considered best for use in suppression GDs due to tighter restriction of Cas9 activity to the germ line (Kyrou et al., 2018; Hammond et al., 2021).
evidence: Described as experimental design in Results and supported by citations

claim: Most knock-in events unexpectedly arose from compound recombinations between the cleaved WT chromosome and both the repair template plasmid and the intact Lp::Sc2A10 sister chromosome.
source: Puzzlingly however, the majority of knock-in larvae contained a compound Lp locus harboring the DsRedNLS-marked GD cassette strictly linked to the GFP-marked Lp::Sc2A10 transgene. Sequencing PCR products spanning parts of this insertion confirmed that, instead of the expected insertion of the Lp-GD cassette, a complex chromosomal rearrangement (Figure 3B) had repaired the Cas9-cleaved wild-type chromosome by incorporating the entire injected plasmid, and by recombining with the intact sister chromosome bearing the Lp::Sc2A10 transgene.
evidence: Demonstrated by sequencing data and genetic linkage analysis described in Results and illustrated in Figure 3B

claim: The GFP-RFP Lp allele was homozygous viable.
source: The resulting unintended transgenic modification at the Lp locus harbored all the components of a classical payload-bearing GD that we hereinafter refer to as GFP-RFP. Similarly to the Lp::Sc2A10 allele, the GFP-RFP Lp allele was homozygous viable, functional Lp protein being expressed from its Lp::Sc2A10 moiety.
evidence: Based on observation of mosquito populations in the laboratory

claim: The GFP-RFP allele was inherited in about 50% of male or female progenies, demonstrating little homing activity after crosses to WT.
source: In spite of the presence of the zpg-Cas9 and gRNA-encoding cassettes in the GFP-RFP allele, it was inherited in about 50% of male or female progenies, demonstrating little homing activity of the GFP-RFP locus after crosses to WT, except for the appearance of rare GFP-only or RFP-only progeny larvae, raising concern about the efficiency of the zpg-Cas9 and/or the gRNA-expressing cassettes.
evidence: Based on genetic crosses and progeny analysis described in Results

claim: Providing an independent copy of vasa-Cas9 on a different chromosome rescued the homing defect and resulted in high homing rates of various segments from the GFP-RFP cassette.
source: Providing an independent copy of vasa-Cas9 on a different chromosome rescued this defect and resulted in high homing rates of various segments from the GFP-RFP cassette (mostly GFP alone, more rarely DsRedNLS alone or both) (Figure 4A), indicating that at least some of the gRNAs in the tRNA-spaced array were active and that the defect was in zpg-Cas9 expression.
evidence: Demonstrated by COPAS data in Figure 4A

claim: Heterozygous mosquitoes carrying one copy of Lp-GD and either GFP-RFP or Lp::Sc2A10 showed a striking developmental delay and died before adulthood.
source: Most heterozygous mosquitoes carrying one copy of Lp-GD and either GFP-RFP or Lp::Sc2A10 (both of which should be refractory to homing of the GD construct) showed a striking developmental delay and died before adulthood (Figure 4B).
evidence: Demonstrated by observation and photograph in Figure 4B

claim: Heterozygous mosquitoes carrying Lp-GD / WT survived to adulthood but were small and short-lived.
source: Heterozygous mosquitoes carrying Lp-GD / WT survived to adulthood but were small and short-lived.
evidence: Based on observation of mosquito populations in the laboratory

claim: WT Lp is largely haplo-insufficient in presence of a Lp loss-of-function allele.
source: These observations indicate that WT Lp is largely haplo-insufficient in presence of a Lp loss-of-function allele, even more so if WT Lp is replaced by Lp::Sc2A10.
evidence: Inferred from developmental delay and lethality data in Figure 4B

claim: It was impossible to create a loss-of function GD in the Lp locus due to haplo-insufficiency of Lp.
source: From the haplo-insufficiency of Lp we concluded that it was impossible to create a loss-of function GD in this locus, precluding an indirect same-locus GD approach.
evidence: Inferred from haplo-insufficiency data

claim: The zpg promoter appeared to have low activity when integrated in the Lp locus.
source: In addition, the zpg promoter appeared to have low activity when integrated in the Lp locus.
evidence: Inferred from low homing rates observed with zpg-Cas9 constructs

claim: Saglin encodes a Plasmodium agonist.
source: To host a GD promoting the spread of Lp::Sc2A10, we turned our attention to the mosquito Saglin locus, which encodes a Plasmodium agonist (Okulate et al., 2007; Ghosh et al., 2009; O'Brochta et al., 2019; Klug et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Okulate et al., 2007; Ghosh et al., 2009; O'Brochta et al., 2019; Klug et al., 2023

claim: The loss of Saglin reduces parasite prevalence and loads, reduces transmission, is homozygous viable and has no obvious fitness cost at least in laboratory conditions.
source: Indeed, while not leading to complete Plasmodium transmission blockage, the loss of Saglin reduces parasite prevalence and loads, reduces transmission, is homozygous viable and has no obvious fitness cost at least in laboratory conditions (Klug et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Klug et al., 2023

claim: A gene drive cassette comprising Cas9 under control of the zpg promoter and an array of 7 gRNAs was inserted disruptively in the endogenous Saglin open reading frame.
source: To exclude that the low zpg-Cas9 activity we previously observed at the Lp locus was due to overlooked mutations in our construct, we subcloned the zpg-Cas9 cassette from a validated GD construct (Kyrou et al., 2018) and incorporated it in a Saglin knock-in plasmid expressing Cas9, DsRedNLS, 3 gRNAs directed against Saglin and 4 gRNAs against Lp (Figure 5, and annotated sequence of this plasmid in Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: Described as experimental design in Results and illustrated in Figure 5A

claim: 100% of the G1 transgenics arising from injected males were females, an indication that the construct had correctly homed onto the X chromosome, where Saglin is located.
source: 100% of the G1 transgenics arising from injected males were females, an indication that the construct had correctly homed onto the X chromosome, where Saglin is located.
evidence: Based on genetic crosses and progeny analysis described in Results

claim: All G1 transgenics had also inherited a copy of Lp::Sc2A10 (GFP positive), instead of the expected 50%.
source: In addition, all G1 transgenics had also inherited a copy of Lp::Sc2A10 (GFP positive), instead of the expected 50%. This suggests that the GD construct acted on the Lp locus, causing either efficient Lp::Sc2A10 homing already in the germ line of G0 males, and/or the death of larvae that did not inherit a protected Lp copy due to the toxicity of the construct's Lp gRNAs.
evidence: Based on genetic crosses and progeny analysis described in Results

claim: The first Saglin GD (SagGDzpg) showed disappointingly modest homing levels at both the Saglin and Lp loci in the G2 generation.
source: In spite of the efficiency of zpg-Cas9 for initial integration, this first Saglin GD (termed SagGDzpg) showed disappointingly modest homing levels at both the Saglin and Lp loci in the G2 generation (Figure 6A).
evidence: Demonstrated by COPAS data in Figure 6A

claim: GFP inheritance was 57.7% (Lp::Sc2A10 locus) compared to 50% expected in the absence of homing.
source: Using COPAS flow cytometry, we examined GFP and DsRed inheritance in 2327 larvae that arose from the pooled G1 females crossed to WT males. It showed 57.7% GFP inheritance (Lp::Sc2A10 locus) compared to 50% expected in the absence of homing.
evidence: Demonstrated by COPAS data in Figure 6A

claim: DsRed inheritance was approximately 54.1% at the Saglin locus.
source: DsRed inheritance was more difficult to assess, as the low intensity of red fluorescence did not allow accurate gating to separate red fluorescent from negative larvae on COPAS diagrams. Approximate gating completed with visual examination of a sample of 200 larvae suggested 54.1% DsRed inheritance at the Saglin locus, an even more modest inheritance bias than for GFP at the Lp locus.
evidence: Demonstrated by COPAS data in Figure 6A

claim: The progeny of triple-transgenic females carrying SagGDzpg, Lp::Sc2A10 and vasa-Cas9 crossed to WT males showed markedly better homing rates (>79% GFP inheritance).
source: To distinguish among these possibilities, we generated females carrying single heterozygous copies of the three unlinked transgenes SagGDzpg, Lp::Sc2A10 and a non-fluorescent (puromycin resistance-marked) vasa-Cas9. The progeny of these triple-transgenic females crossed to WT males showed markedly better homing rates (>79% GFP inheritance) (Figure 6B).
evidence: Demonstrated by COPAS data in Figure 6B

claim: vasa-Cas9 was able to significantly rescue the modest homing rate of zpg-Cas9 from SagGDzpg, resulting in an efficient split GD.
source: Thus, vasa-Cas9 was able to significantly rescue the modest homing rate of zpg-Cas9 from SagGDzpg, resulting in an efficient split GD.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of homing rates in Figures 6A and 6B

claim: The cloned zpg promoter sequence is sensitive to positional effects, being poorly active when inserted in Saglin or Lp in contrast to other previously reported host loci such as DSX or Nudel.
source: This suggests that the cloned zpg promoter sequence is sensitive to positional effects, being poorly active when inserted in Saglin or Lp in contrast to other previously reported host loci such as DSX or Nudel (Kyrou et al., 2018; Hammond et al., 2021).
evidence: Inferred from homing rate data and supported by citations

claim: One mosquito population of Lp::Sc2A10 combined with SagGDzpg showed an increase in the frequency of both alleles after seven generations (G7: GFP allelic frequency = 59.2%, phenotypic expression of DsRed in >90% of larvae, n=4282 larvae).
source: We maintained one mosquito population of Lp::Sc2A10 combined with SagGDzpg (initial allele frequencies: 25% and 33%, respectively) and measured genotype frequencies after seven generations. This showed an increase in the frequency of both alleles (G7: GFP allelic frequency = 59.2%, phenotypic expression of DsRed in >90% of larvae, n=4282 larvae), indicating that the modest GD strength of SagGDzpg was still able to increase the frequency of the SagGDzpg allele over time and counteract the Lp::Sc2A10 fitness cost.
evidence: Based on COPAS analysis of mosquito populations over generations

claim: Two versions of SagGDvasa were initially made: one carrying a complex array of seven gRNAs and another carrying six tandem U6-gRNA units.
source: We initially made two versions of SagGDvasa: one carrying the complex array of seven gRNAs described above for SagGDzpg (as in Figure 5A); another carrying six tandem U6-gRNA units (Figure 5B; sequence provided in Supplementary file 1E).
evidence: Described as experimental design in Results and illustrated in Figure 5

claim: About 20 DsRed positive G1 females and no positive male were recovered from outcrossing G0 injected males to WT females, again an indication of proper insertion of the GD cassette onto the X chromosome.
source: About 35 surviving G0 injected male mosquitoes (which were homozygous for Lp::Sc2A10 to prevent any premature damage on Lp), outcrossed to WT females, yielded about 20 DsRed positive G1 females and no positive male, again an indication of proper insertion of the GD cassette onto the X chromosome, where Saglin is located.
evidence: Based on genetic crosses and progeny analysis described in Results

claim: G1 females heterozygous at both SagGDvasa on the X chromosome and Lp::Sc2A10 on the second chromosome developed normally to adulthood and were fertile when crossed to wild-type males.
source: These G1 females (heterozygous at both SagGDvasa on the X chromosome and Lp::Sc2A10 on the second chromosome) developed normally to adulthood and were fertile when crossed to wild-type males.
evidence: Based on observation of mosquito populations in the laboratory

claim: High homing rates at both loci were recorded in G2 by examining the progeny of the individual G1 females backcrossed to WT males, a large majority of progeny inheriting both a SagGDvasa copy (DsRedNLS) and a Lp::Sc2A10 copy (GFP).
source: High homing rates at both loci were recorded in G2 by examining the progeny of the individual G1 females backcrossed to WT males, a large majority of progeny inheriting both a SagGDvasa copy (DsRedNLS) and a Lp::Sc2A10 copy (GFP) (Table 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by genetic crosses and progeny analysis in Table 2

claim: The male cross yielded only 405 larvae, of which 391 were GFP positive (GFP inheritance: 96.5%, corresponding to a homing rate of 93%).
source: The male cross yielded only 405 larvae, of which 391 were GFP positive (GFP inheritance: 96.5%, corresponding to a homing rate of 93%).
evidence: Based on COPAS analysis of progeny from genetic crosses

claim: The female cross yielded 5197 larvae showing 95.1% GFP inheritance and 80.7% DsRed inheritance, corresponding to homing rates of 90.2% at the Lp locus and 61.4% at the Saglin locus.
source: The female cross yielded 5197 larvae showing 95.1% GFP inheritance and 80.7% DsRed inheritance, corresponding to homing rates of 90.2% at the Lp locus and 61.4% at the Saglin locus.
evidence: Based on COPAS analysis of progeny from genetic crosses

claim: The vasa promoter was highly active in germ cells when inserted in the Saglin locus.
source: Thus, in contrast to zpg, the vasa promoter was highly active in germ cells when inserted in the Saglin locus.
evidence: Inferred from high homing rates observed with vasa-Cas9 constructs

claim: Saglin was undetectable in SagGDvasa mosquitoes by western blotting.
source: To verify that SagGDvasa abolished Saglin expression, we dissected salivary glands from control and homozygous DsRed +mosquito females, and subjected them to western blotting using anti-Saglin antibodies. As expected, Saglin was undetectable in SagGDvasa mosquitoes (Figure 5C).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot data in Figure 5C

claim: In all populations, mosquitoes lacking Lp::Sc2A10 disappeared rapidly, and all young populations rapidly consisted of a majority of homozygous Lp::Sc2A10 mosquitoes.
source: In all populations, mosquitoes lacking Lp::Sc2A10 disappeared rapidly, and all young populations rapidly consisted of a majority of homozygous Lp::Sc2A10 mosquitoes (Figure 7 and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Demonstrated by COPAS data in Figure 7 and Supplementary file 5

claim: DsRed-only individuals were strikingly absent from all early populations, indicative of the lethality of the SagGDvasa transgene in the absence of a protected Lp allele.
source: Despite the absence of physical linkage between the two transgenes, DsRed-only individuals were strikingly absent from all early populations, indicative of the lethality of the SagGDvasa transgene in the absence of a protected Lp allele.
evidence: Demonstrated by COPAS data in Figure 7 and Supplementary file 5

claim: Toxicity of SagGDvasa was due to its destructive action on the Lp locus rather than to a fitness cost of its disrupted Saglin host locus.
source: Importantly, toxicity of SagGDvasa was due to its destructive action on the Lp locus rather than to a fitness cost of its disrupted Saglin host locus, since individuals carrying both DsRed and GFP thrived in all populations, and consistent with the reported absence of obvious fitness cost of Saglin mutants (Klug et al., 2023).
evidence: Inferred from population dynamics data and supported by citation to Klug et al., 2023

claim: Several populations (notably populations 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7) rapidly seemed fixed for Lp::Sc2A10.
source: Several populations (notably populations 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7) rapidly seemed fixed for Lp::Sc2A10.
evidence: Demonstrated by COPAS data in Figure 7 and Supplementary file 5

claim: A trend for reversal, with Lp::Sc2A10 progressively giving way to GFP negative individuals, was observed from G14 on for population 2.
source: A trend for reversal, with Lp::Sc2A10 progressively giving way to GFP negative individuals (presumably functional Lp mutants refractory to homing), was observed from G14 on for population 2, although GFP positive individuals still represented a large majority of the population (>90% from G1 on), while GFP allele frequency reached 0.98 at G8 before decreasing and oscillating between 0.71 and 0.92 after G14.
evidence: Demonstrated by COPAS data in Figure 7 and Supplementary file 5

claim: A substantial fraction of DsRed negative individuals (up to 30%), likely carrying GD refractory Saglin mutants, persisted in some populations.
source: While the majority of mosquitoes of all populations rapidly carried at least one copy of SagGDvasa, we observed that a substantial fraction of DsRed negative individuals (up to 30%), likely carrying GD refractory Saglin mutants, persisted in some populations (Figure 7 and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Demonstrated by COPAS data in Figure 7 and Supplementary file 5

claim: DsRed negative mosquitoes represented 18 and 31% of populations 1 and 2, respectively, at the generations sampled.
source: To characterize Saglin mutants, we COPAS-extracted 750 and 150 DsRed-negative larvae from a surplus of larvae from generation 4 of population 1 and generation 3 of population 2. DsRed-negative individuals represented 18 and 31% of these populations, respectively, with the Saglin gene on their X chromosome having been exposed to between one and four rounds of Cas9 activity.
evidence: Based on COPAS analysis of mosquito populations

claim: The majority of sequenced DsRed negative alleles still corresponded to wild-type Saglin having thus far escaped GD activity.
source: While the majority of sequenced DsRed negative alleles still corresponded to wild-type Saglin having thus far escaped GD activity, a wide variety of Saglin mutations, different between the two sampled populations, were readily identified (Figure 8a and b).
evidence: Demonstrated by high-throughput sequencing data in Figure 8A and B

claim: A majority of Saglin haplotypes were mutated only at the target site of gRNA2, suggesting that this gRNA was the most active of the three.
source: Interestingly, a majority of these Saglin haplotypes were mutated only at the target site of gRNA2, suggesting that this gRNA was the most active of the three and that Cas9, confronted to a pool of three Saglin and three Lp gRNAs, will not necessarily cleave all target sites in a given germ cell.
evidence: Inferred from high-throughput sequencing data in Figure 8A and B

claim: Deletions spanning two gRNA target sites were rare in the samples (one instance of such a haplotype was detected, carrying a deletion between gRNA1 and gRNA2).
source: Deletions spanning two gRNA target sites were rare in our samples (one instance of such a haplotype was detected, carrying a deletion between gRNA1 and gRNA2).
evidence: Demonstrated by high-throughput sequencing data in Figure 8A and B

claim: At least one haplotype with mutations in all three target sites was recovered after four generations.
source: Inexorably however, Saglin mutants fully refractory to the GD will form in mosquito populations; we recovered at least one haplotype with mutations in all three target sites after four generations (Figure 8a).
evidence: Demonstrated by high-throughput sequencing data in Figure 8A

claim: A few GFP negative larvae appeared in populations 2 and 3, amounting to 2.4% of total larvae in generation 14 of population 2.
source: While tracking the frequency of transgenes in [SagGDvasa; Lp::Sc2A10] mosquitoes, we noted the appearance of a few GFP negative larvae in populations 2 and 3. These amounted to 2.4% of total larvae in generation 14 of population 2.
evidence: Based on COPAS analysis of mosquito populations

claim: GFP negative mosquitoes developed to healthy and fertile adults.
source: We COPAS-isolated a sample of these larvae and grew them to adulthood, expecting that they might die during development due to unrescued deleterious mutations in Lp. However, these GFP negative mosquitoes developed to healthy and fertile adults.
evidence: Based on observation of mosquito populations in the laboratory

claim: Sequencing the Lp gene in 12 GFP negative individuals revealed that all were homozygous for the same array of mutations within two of the three Lp gRNA target sequences.
source: Sequencing the Lp gene in 12 individuals revealed that all were homozygous for the same array of mutations within two of the three Lp gRNA target sequences (Figure 8c).
evidence: Demonstrated by sequencing data in Figure 8C

claim: One mutation deleted three nucleotides before the PAM of gRNA2, removing a single valine from the Lp signal peptide.
source: One mutation deleted three nucleotides before the PAM of gRNA2, removing a single valine from the Lp signal peptide (MWVLGGRRLLWSFLVSLVLIQSVSA, missing valine underlined).
evidence: Demonstrated by sequencing data in Figure 8C

claim: The other mutation is a 5-base deletion within the target of gRNA3 in the first Lp intron.
source: The other is a 5-base deletion within the target of gRNA3 in the first Lp intron.
evidence: Demonstrated by sequencing data in Figure 8C

claim: Viability of the homozygous mutant indicates that this combination of mutations, while rendering Lp refractory to Cas9-mediated gene conversion, preserved Lp function.
source: Viability of the homozygous mutant indicates that this combination of mutations, while rendering Lp refractory to Cas9-mediated gene conversion, preserved Lp function.
evidence: Inferred from viability data and sequencing data in Figure 8C

claim: The first of the three gRNA expressed from the gRNA array did not act.
source: This suggested that (i) the first of the three gRNA expressed from the gRNA array did not act; and (ii) combinations of mutations preserving the function of target essential genes can emerge despite the cumulative activity of two gRNAs, which in this case was certainly facilitated by the fact that one of them targeted an intron, more permissive to change.
evidence: Inferred from sequencing data in Figure 8C and gRNA array structure

claim: Two derivative alleles of the gene drive construct dominated the four sampled mosquito populations: a longer version that still retained five of the original six gRNAs, and a shorter version that retained only two gRNAs.
source: Interestingly, two derivative alleles of the gene drive construct dominated the four sampled mosquito populations: a longer version that still retained five of the original six gRNAs, and a shorter version that retained only two gRNAs.
evidence: Demonstrated by PCR and sequencing data in Figure 9

claim: The original transgenesis vector used for microinjection was resequenced and verified to contain all six gRNA expression units; therefore, deletions occurred post integration in the mosquito genome.
source: The original transgenesis vector used for microinjection was resequenced and verified to contain all six gRNA expression units; therefore, deletions occurred post integration in the mosquito genome.
evidence: Based on sequencing of the original plasmid and comparison to PCR products from mosquitoes

claim: The same deletion of the first Lp gRNA was detected in both populations 1 and 2, separated at the third generation following transgenesis and subsequently bred independently for 29 generations before sampling.
source: gRNA deletions probably began to occur early in the evolution of the transgenic populations, since the same deletion of the first Lp gRNA was detected in both populations 1 and 2, separated at the third generation following transgenesis and subsequently bred independently for 29 generations before sampling.
evidence: Demonstrated by PCR and sequencing data in Figure 9

claim: The Cas9 part of the transgene appeared to be intact in mosquitoes with deleted gRNA arrays.
source: Regardless of the number of missing gRNA units, the Cas9 part of the transgene appeared to be intact in these mosquitoes (Figure 9C).
evidence: Demonstrated by PCR data in Figure 9C

claim: All four mice exposed on day 18 to infected control females developed parasitemia, whereas all six mice exposed to infected transgenics remained negative.
source: Seventeen days later, females carrying visible GFP parasites were selected and split into six cups of 10 transgenic, and four cups of 10 WT. All four mice exposed on day 18 to the infected control females developed parasitemia, whereas all six mice exposed to infected transgenics remained negative (Supplementary file 4D).
evidence: Demonstrated by bite-back experiment data in Supplementary file 4D

claim: Only two of six mice developed parasitemia 6 days after infection when exposed to 8–12 bites from [SagGDvasa; Lp::Sc2A10] oocyst-carrying females of the 4th generation of population 6.
source: Six additional mice were exposed to 8–12 bites from [SagGDvasa; Lp::Sc2A10] oocyst-carrying females of the 4th generation of population 6, corresponding to the 23rdgeneration since transgenesis. Only two of these six mice developed parasitemia 6 days after infection (Supplementary file 4E).
evidence: Demonstrated by bite-back experiment data in Supplementary file 4E

claim: [SagGDvasa; Lp::Sc2A10] mosquitoes maintained a markedly decreased ability to transmit Plasmodium after >20 generations of existence.
source: While the small scale of these experiments cannot strictly confirm whether the Saglin knockout enhanced protection against transmission (especially as in these experiments we discarded less-infected mosquitoes, which are expected to result from Saglin loss-of-function), the absence of infection in a total of 10 out of 12 mice, in contrast to 4 mice out of 4 infected when exposed to infected WT mosquitoes (Figure 2D), showed that [SagGDvasa; Lp::Sc2A10] mosquitoes maintained a markedly decreased ability to transmit Plasmodium after >20 generations of existence.
evidence: Inferred from bite-back experiment data in Supplementary files 4D and 4E and Figure 2D

claim: The 2A10 antibody targets a highly repeated epitope on the CSP protein (the NANP motif), that is conserved across P. falciparum strains.
source: However, the 2A10 antibody targets a highly repeated epitope on the CSP protein (the NANP motif), that, in addition to being repetitive, is also conserved across P. falciparum strains.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the Discussion

claim: CSP is required in several processes in the sporozoite's journey between two hosts.
source: A combination of mutations leading to the complete loss of this epitope in Plasmodium therefore seems unlikely, and would probably cause a dramatic loss of parasite fitness as CSP is required in several processes in the sporozoite's journey between two hosts (Coppi et al., 2011; Balaban et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Coppi et al., 2011 and Balaban et al., 2021

claim: The zpg promoter is sensitive to positional effects and its usability in GD constructs may be restricted to a subset of genomic loci.
source: Interestingly, the zpg promoter that in theory possesses this advantage showed low activity once inserted in the Lp and Saglin loci, in contrast to the DSX or Nudel loci (Hammond et al., 2016; Kyrou et al., 2018). This suggests that the zpg promoter is more sensitive to the local chromatin context than the vasa2 promoter, similarly to the sds3 promoter in Aedes aegypti (Anderson et al., 2023), and that its usability in GD constructs may be restricted to a subset of genomic loci.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and supported by citations

claim: The genetic design established here can be viewed as a two-component GD in which one component (Lp::Sc2A10) has no drive capacity by itself but (i) rescues the lethality, and (ii) hitchhikes on the drive capacity of the other (SagGDvasa) ensuring its own hyper-Mendelian spread.
source: The genetic design established here can be viewed as a two-component GD in which one component (Lp::Sc2A10) has no drive capacity by itself but (i) rescues the lethality, and (ii) hitchhikes on the drive capacity of the other (SagGDvasa) ensuring its own hyper-Mendelian spread.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing reciprocal dependence of the two transgenes

claim: The two transgenic loci are reciprocally dependent on each other: Lp::Sc2A10 depends on SagGD for its long-term persistence and spread in a population, and SagGD depends on Lp::Sc2A10 as a rescue allele of the essential Lp target for its survival.
source: The two transgenic loci are, therefore, reciprocally dependent on each other: Lp::Sc2A10 depends on SagGD for its long-term persistence and spread in a population, and SagGD depends on Lp::Sc2A10 as a rescue allele of the essential Lp target for its survival.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing reciprocal dependence of the two transgenes

claim: This design can be seen as a two-locus variation of rescue-type GDs.
source: This design can be seen as a two-locus variation of rescue-type GDs (Adolfi et al., 2020; Champer et al., 2020a).
evidence: Inferred from experimental design and supported by citations

claim: A novel P. berghei strain combining the strong GFP fluorescence of Δp230p-GFP with the substitution of endogenous P. berghei CSP for CSP from P. falciparum was generated.
source: We generated a novel P. berghei strain combining the strong GFP fluorescence of Δp230p-GFP (Manzoni et al., 2014) with the substitution of endogenous P. berghei CSP for CSP from P. falciparum from strain Pb-PfCSP (Triller et al., 2017), in which GFP fluorescence was too faint for selecting live infected mosquitoes examined under 488 nm light.
evidence: Described as experimental method in Materials and methods
